ranked_results.content: Due to time constraints, course instructors often need to selectively participate in student discussion threads, due to their limited bandwidth and lopsided student--instructor ratio on online forums. We propose the first deep learning models for this binary prediction problem. We propose novel attention based models to infer the amount of latent context necessary to predict instructor intervention. Such models also allow themselves to be tuned to instructor's preference to intervene early or late. Our three proposed attentive model variants to infer the latent context improve over the state-of-the-art by a significant, large margin of 11% in F1 and 10% in recall, on average. Further, introspection of attention help us better understand what aspects of a discussion post propagate through the discussion thread that prompts instructor intervention.

ranked_results.content: We predict instructor intervention on student discussions by first inferring the optimal size of the context needed to decide on the intervention decision for the intervened post. We first show that a structured representation of the complete thread as the context is better than a bag-of-words, feature-rich representation. We then propose attention-based models to infer and select a context – defined as a contiguous subsequence of student posts – to improve over a model that always takes the complete thread as a context to prediction intervention. Our Any Post Attention (APA) model enables instructors to tune the model to predict intervention early or late. We posit our APA model will enable MOOC instructors employing varying pedagogical styles to use the model equally well. We introspect the attention models' performance across threads of varying lengths and show that APA predicts intervention on longer threads, which possesses more candidate contexts, better.

ranked_results.content: When they intervene, instructors either pay attention to a specific post or a series of posts, which trigger their reply. However, instructors rarely explicitly indicate to which post(s) their intervention is in relation to. This is the case in our corpus, party due to Coursera's user interface which only allows for single level comments (see Figure FIGREF2 ). Based solely on the binary, thread-level intervention signal, our secondary objective seeks to infer the appropriate context – represented by a sequence of posts – as the basis for the intervention.

ranked_results.content: In this paper, we improve the state-of-the-art for instructor intervention in MOOC forums. We propose the first neural models for this prediction problem. We show that modelling the thread structure and the sequence of posts explicitly improves performance. Instructors in different MOOCs from different subject areas intervene differently. For example, on a Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM) MOOC, instructors may often intervene early as possible to resolve misunderstanding of the subject material and prevent confusion. However, in a Humanities MOOC, instructors allow for the students to explore open-ended discussions and debate among themselves. Such instructors may prefer to intervene later in the discussion to encourage further discussion or resolve conflicts among students. We therefore propose attention models to infer the latent context, i.e., the series of posts that trigger an intervention. Earlier studies on MOOC forum intervention either model the entire context or require the context size to be specified explicitly.

ranked_results.content: Recent work in deep neural modeling has used an attention mechanism as a focusing query to highlight specific items within the input history that significantly influence the current decision point. Our work employs this mechanism – but with a twist: due to the fact that the actual instructor intervention is not (yet) available at the decision timing, we cannot use any actual intervention to decide the context. To employ attention, we must then employ a surrogate text as the query to train our prediction model. Our model variants model assess the suitability of such surrogate texts for the attention mechanism basis.

Instructors (defined here as the course instructors, their teaching assistants and the MOOC platform's technical staff) monitor the discussion forum to post (reply to their message) in discussion threads among students. We refer to this posting as intervention, following prior work BIBREF0 . However, due to large student enrolment, the student–instructor ratio in MOOCs is very high Therefore, instructors are not able to monitor and participate in all student discussions. To address this problem, a number of works have proposed systems e.g., BIBREF0 , BIBREF1 to aid instructors to selectively intervene on student discussions where they are needed the most.

ranked_results.content:
**Summary: Deep Learning Models for Instructor Intervention Prediction in MOOC Discussion Forums**

---

**Background & Problem Statement:**

Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs) scale education globally but suffer from a critical communication gap: instructors cannot monitor or respond to all student discussions due to high student-to-instructor ratios and limited bandwidth. To address this, instructors selectively intervene in discussion threads — defined as posting replies — to guide learning, resolve confusion, or manage conflicts. However, existing systems either lack structure-aware modeling or require manual context specification, limiting generalizability and performance. The problem is framed as a **binary classification task**: predict whether an instructor will intervene (1) or not (0) in a given discussion thread, based on the sequence of posts prior to any intervention. A key challenge is **inferring the appropriate latent context** — the contiguous sequence of posts that most likely triggers an intervention — without knowing the instructor’s reply in advance. ---

**Key Innovations:**

1. **First Deep Learning Models for Instructor Intervention Prediction:**
   - Propose the first neural architectures specifically designed for this binary prediction problem. - Introduce **attention-based models** to dynamically infer the optimal context length and content that triggers instructor intervention. 2. **Context Inference via Attention Mechanisms:**
   - Unlike prior work that either models the entire context or requires pre-defined context lengths, the proposed models **learn context dynamically**. - Attention mechanisms are used to weigh the importance of different posts in the thread sequence, enabling the model to focus on the most relevant prior content. 3. **Three Novel Attention-Based Model Variants:**
   - **Ultimate Post Attention (UPA)**: Uses the most recent post (just before intervention) as a query to attend to the full context. Assumes intervention is triggered by the latest content. - **Penultimate Post Attention (PPA)**: Uses the second-to-last post as the query, allowing the model to consider broader context while still leveraging recent information. - **Any Post Attention (APA)**: Generalizes further — each post in the thread acts as a query to attend to its preceding context, enabling the model to consider interventions triggered by any point in the thread. 4. **Hierarchical LSTM Architecture (hLSTM):**
   - Encodes each post using pre-trained GloVe word vectors passed through an LSTM to generate a “post vector.”
   - The thread is then encoded hierarchically: each post’s vector is fed into a second LSTM to capture thread-level context. - Hidden states at each step represent the context after each post, enabling dynamic context inference. 5. **Surrogate Query for Attention:**
   - Since the instructor’s reply is not available at prediction time, the model uses the **most recent post (or any prior post)** as a surrogate query to compute attention weights over the thread history. - This allows the model to learn what content in the thread is most likely to prompt intervention, without needing the actual intervention text. 6. **Instructor Style Adaptation:**
   - Models are designed to be **tunable to instructor preferences** — early intervention (e.g., in STEM courses to prevent misunderstanding) vs. late intervention (e.g., in Humanities to encourage debate). - Attention mechanisms implicitly capture these preferences by learning which parts of the thread are most predictive of intervention based on domain-specific discourse patterns. ---

**Performance & Evaluation:**

- Evaluated on a **diverse corpus of 12 MOOC iterations** from Coursera.org, covering varying sizes, instructor styles, and intervention patterns. - Data preprocessing: 
  - Threads restricted to subject-specific sub-forums (Lecture, Homework, Quiz, Exam). - Excluded social or announcement threads. - URLs, equations, and timestamps replaced with tokens. - Truncated intervened threads to posts before the first instructor reply to avoid bias. - **Metrics**: F1 and Recall scores reported on the positive class (interventions). - **Results**:
  - All three attention models **significantly outperform state-of-the-art**. - **Average improvement of 11% in F1 and 10% in Recall** — a large, statistically significant margin. - Models generalize across MOOCs and instructor styles without requiring context length specification. ---

**Comparative Advantages:**

- **No pre-defined context length**: Unlike prior models (e.g., BIBREF0, BIBREF4), attention mechanisms dynamically infer context scope. - **No reliance on explicit reply structure**: Unlike BIBREF5 (graph-LSTM), models do not assume tree-like reply structures — Coursera’s interface doesn’t support them, and users often misdirect replies. - **Hierarchical encoding**: Combines post-level and thread-level representations, capturing both local content and global thread dynamics. - **Surrogate query mechanism**: Enables attention-based context inference without needing the intervention text — a critical constraint in real-time prediction. ---

**Insights from Attention Mechanisms:**

- **Introspection of attention weights** reveals which parts of the thread (e.g., questions, clarifications, disagreements) are most likely to trigger intervention. - Helps explain **why** instructors intervene — e.g., unresolved confusion, emotional tone, or consensus-seeking behavior. - Enables **actionable insights** for MOOC platforms to recommend intervention points or flag high-risk threads. ---

**Limitations & Future Work:**

- Models assume linear, contiguous contexts — which is valid for MOOC forums but may not generalize to forums with tree-like structures (e.g., Reddit). - Does not model instructor intent beyond intervention likelihood — future work could incorporate sentiment, tone, or pedagogical goals. - Evaluation is limited to Coursera — future work should test on other platforms and languages.
